The church is full of people. I do not like the road. I do not like the people. I like the voles. I like the mice. I like the frogs. I like the water. I like the trees.

I drink where the dew is. On the ivy, or the bramble, or the hawthorn. I wait for the night to cool, then I drink. It's the only time I can do it without the cold getting me. I don't like the rain. It makes me wet and the water tastes bad. I prefer the dew. It's clean. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hear the stream from the moor, but not at night. The water is too cold and dark. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the call of the barn owl, and the creak of the old oak. The stream is a memory from the day.

I hear the stream from my roost. It runs through the moor, just beyond the old oak. The water is cold and clear, and it sings at night. I can hear the ripple of it, the splash of fish, and the call of the water rat. Sometimes I hear the water from the wood, when the wind carries it. It is a sound I know well. I do not drink from it, but I listen.

A stream. The one that runs through the moor, past the lane, and into the ditch by the barn. I can hear it from my tree, and I can see it when the light is right. It's where the water comes from, and where the voles go to drink. I don't like it much. Too cold. Too wet. But it's where the food is.

The road is wide and noisy, with lights and voices. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where it is quiet and the air is still. The moor is not my place. I have no need to go beyond.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find. Voles, mice, shrews, moles, beetles, worms, slugs, even a small bird if it is slow. I do not choose. I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the roots and under the leaves. I sit still, listening for the rustle of their feet. When I hear it, I fly down and strike. I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, even a small bird if it's not too big. I don't chew. I just swallow it whole, and then I digest it. It's how I get the nutrients I need. I don't eat anything else. I don't even eat the bones. I just leave them in the hollow.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them in the soil, and I strike. They are the main part of my diet. I also catch mice, shrews, and sometimes a young rabbit if it's small. But voles are the most common.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's narrow, just wide enough for me to turn my head. The bark is rough and smells of damp earth. I sleep in it at night, and I watch the road from the top of the tree. The wind sometimes howls through the branches, and the rain makes the leaves drip. I know every crack and every branch. It's where I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I roost in the dark and the wind sings through the leaves. I have been here for years, and the tree knows me. I can hear the stream from here, and the road with its lights at night. The hollow is safe, and I keep it warm with my wings.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, and I have a small chamber inside. I can hear the wind through the branches, and sometimes the rain. I sleep there at night, and I watch the moor from the top of the tree. The owlets are in the nest, and I keep them warm. I am safe here, and I am not alone.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's a narrow, round hole, just big enough for me to squeeze through. The bark is rough and smells of damp earth. I line it with moss and feathers. I sleep there at night, and I watch the wood from the inside. The wind howls through the branches, and sometimes I hear the plop of a mouse in the undergrowth. I am safe here, and I am never far from the oak.
